content: Japanese encephalitis (JE) is a viral infection of the brain and central nervous system caused by the Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV), a flavivirus. The virus is transmitted to humans through the bite of infected mosquitoes, primarily of the Culex species, particularly Culex tritaeniorhynchus. The virus is maintained in nature through a cycle involving mosquitoes and vertebrate hosts, mainly pigs and water birds. Humans are incidental hosts and are considered dead-end hosts because they do not develop high enough levels of the virus in their bloodstream to infect mosquitoes. The incubation period for JE is typically 5–15 days. Most individuals infected with JEV remain asymptomatic, making it challenging to determine the true incidence of the disease. It is estimated that less than 1% of infected individuals develop clinical disease. However, when symptoms do occur, they can be severe. Approximately 1 in 250 infections results in severe clinical illness, characterized by the sudden onset of high fever, headache, neck stiffness, altered mental status, disorientation, coma, seizures (especially in children), limb weakness, spastic paralysis, and, in some cases, death. The case fatality rate among those with severe symptoms can reach up to 30%, with an estimated 13,600–20,400 deaths annually. Among survivors, 20–30% experience permanent neurological, intellectual, or behavioral sequelae, such as paralysis, recurrent seizures, or speech impairments. JE is a significant public health concern due to its severe morbidity and mortality, as well as its expanding global distribution. It is the leading cause of viral encephalitis in tropical regions. Currently, most cases are reported from the WHO South-East Asia Region (approximately 60%) and the Western Pacific Region (about 40%). However, individuals of any age can be affected. Vaccination is the most effective method for preventing JE. JE vaccination should be integrated into national immunization schedules in areas where the disease is recognized as a public health priority. There are four main types of JE vaccines currently in use: inactivated mouse brain-derived vaccines (production halted in 2006), inactivated Vero cell-derived vaccines (administered in two doses, four weeks apart, starting at six months of age in endemic areas), live attenuated vaccines (single dose, administered from eight months of age), and live recombinant (chimeric) vaccines (single dose, administered from nine months of age). All current JE vaccines are derived from genotype III strains but provide protective immunity against other genotypes. Surveillance data on JE is critical for guiding public health policies and strategies. It helps assess the impact of vaccination programs, identify high-risk populations or geographic areas, monitor the performance of surveillance and laboratory systems, and evaluate vaccine effectiveness. Surveillance systems should aim for high reporting completeness and timeliness, adequate specimen collection, and proper laboratory testing. For example, at least 80% of surveillance units should report to the national level on time, even in the absence of cases. The public health response to JE includes vaccination, health education, and supportive case management. Community awareness is essential to reduce delays in seeking medical care after symptom onset. Immediate supportive care for JE cases can reduce mortality. While human vaccination is the only proven method for reducing JE disease, there is limited evidence to support other interventions, such as pig vaccination, environmental management for vector control, or chemical vector control. JE is endemic in 24 countries across the WHO South-East Asia and Western Pacific regions, exposing over 3 billion people to the risk of infection. The annual incidence of clinical disease varies widely, ranging from less than 1 to more than 10 cases per 100,000 population during outbreaks. The disease burden is estimated at 68,000 clinical cases annually, making JEV the most important cause of viral encephalitis in many Asian countries.
